sections.title: What are Matrix Operations?
sections.content:
Matrices appear in DSA in two distinct contexts. The first — 2D grids for BFS/DFS — is covered in the 2D Arrays topic. The second is matrices as **mathematical objects** supporting multiplication, which unlocks powerful algorithms for linear recurrences and path counting.

**Matrix exponentiation** computes M^k using repeated squaring: the same idea as fast modular exponentiation. Each squaring step halves the exponent, so M^k requires only O(log k) multiplications. For small matrices (2×2 or 3×3), each multiplication is effectively O(1), making the entire computation O(log k). This transforms computing the nth Fibonacci number from O(n) to O(log n).

The deeper insight: **any linear recurrence** of order d can be represented as matrix multiplication on a d-dimensional state vector. Raise the transition matrix to the (n-1)th power and multiply by the initial state. Works for Fibonacci, Tribonacci, any recurrence `f(n) = a1*f(n-1) + a2*f(n-2) + ...`

Matrix exponentiation also solves **graph path counting**: the (i,j) entry of the adjacency matrix raised to the kth power gives the number of walks of exactly length k from node i to node j.

The second cluster is **grid transformations**: rotating a matrix 90 degrees (transpose + row reverse), reflecting it, spiral traversal.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Reach for matrix exponentiation when a problem asks for the nth term of a linear recurrence with large n (where O(n) is too slow), or counting graph paths of exact length k. Use grid transformation techniques for matrix rotation, reflection, and spiral traversal problems.

sections.title: Matrix Multiplication, Exponentiation, and Grid Operations
sections.content:
## Matrix Multiplication

`C[i][j] = sum over k of A[i][k] * B[k][j]`. O(n³) for n×n matrices.

Key properties: **associative** (A×B×C = A×(B×C)) — this makes exponentiation valid. **NOT commutative** (A×B ≠ B×A). Identity matrix I has 1s on diagonal, 0s elsewhere. M×I = M.

## Matrix Exponentiation

```
matpow(M, k):
  if k===0: return identity
  if k even: half=matpow(M,k/2); return half×half
  if k odd: return M×matpow(M,k-1)
```
O(log k) multiplications, each O(n³).

## Fibonacci via Matrix

`[[F(n+1)],[F(n)]] = [[1,1],[1,0]]^n × [[F(1)],[F(0)]]`

Raise the 2×2 transition matrix to the nth power to get F(n) in O(log n).

## Any Linear Recurrence

For `f(n) = a*f(n-1) + b*f(n-2) + c*f(n-3)`, build a 3×3 transition matrix. First row encodes coefficients; remaining rows shift state. Raise to (n-3)th power, multiply by initial state vector.

## Graph Path Counting

`A^k[i][j]` = number of walks of exactly length k from node i to j where A is the adjacency matrix.

## Grid Operations

**Rotate 90° clockwise**: transpose (swap A[i][j] and A[j][i] for j > i) then reverse each row.
**Spiral traversal**: maintain four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right), peel one layer per cycle.

sections.title: Diagonal Traversal Techniques
sections.content:
Two different groupings of matrix cells by diagonal come up repeatedly, and it's worth knowing both explicitly rather than re-deriving them each time:

**Same anti-diagonal (top-right to bottom-left)**: all cells `(i, j)` where `i + j` is constant share the same anti-diagonal. Grouping cells by `i + j` into buckets (an array of length `rows + cols - 1`, or a hash map) is the standard first step for 'diagonal traversal' style problems where you need to process the matrix diagonal-by-diagonal rather than row-by-row.

**Same main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right)**: all cells `(i, j)` where `i - j` is constant share the same main diagonal. This grouping is what makes 'is this matrix Toeplitz' (every diagonal has the same value throughout) checkable in one pass - just verify `matrix[i][j] === matrix[i-1][j-1]` for every cell not in the first row/column, which is really checking that every `i - j` group has a single consistent value without needing to build the groups explicitly at all.

Both groupings turn a 2D traversal-order problem into a simpler 1D indexing problem (index by `i+j` or `i-j` instead of `(i, j)` directly) - recognizing which of the two a problem needs (anti-diagonal for zigzag/diagonal-order traversal, main diagonal for Toeplitz-style same-diagonal-value checks) is usually the entire trick.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Generic matrix exponentiation kernel with optional modular arithmetic. Includes Fibonacci specialization and in-place 90-degree rotation as grid operation reference.

items.name: Higher-Order Recurrences
items.description: For order-d recurrences, build a d×d transition matrix. First row encodes coefficients, remaining rows shift state. Raise to (n-d)th power and multiply by initial d-element state vector.

items.name: Graph Path Counting via Adjacency Matrix
items.description: Build adjacency matrix A. A^k[i][j] gives walks of exactly length k from i to j. Combine with modular exponentiation for k up to 10^18.

items.name: Grid Rotation and Spiral Traversal
items.description: Rotate Image requires in-place 90-degree rotation via transpose + row reverse. Spiral Matrix requires four-boundary peeling. Both test spatial reasoning and careful index management.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n³ log k) for matrix exponentiation of n×n matrix to kth power
sections.explanation: Each matrix multiplication is O(n³). Fast exponentiation performs O(log k) multiplications. For Fibonacci n=2 so this is O(log k) effectively. Grid transformations (rotate, spiral) visit each cell a constant number of times: O(n²).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative — in the exponentiation loop, always apply result = result × base to maintain the correct power accumulation invariant.
Identity matrix has 1s on the diagonal and 0s everywhere else. Using the zero matrix as identity causes M × I = zero matrix.
Off-by-one in exponent for Fibonacci: raise T to the (n-1)th power, not nth. Verify manually with n=2: T^1 × [F(1), F(0)] should give [F(2), F(1)].
Missing modular arithmetic inside matrix multiplication: each element accumulates up to n products of large values. Take mod after each addition in the inner loop, not just at the end.
Grid rotation: transpose requires iterating j > i only (upper triangle). Iterating all (i,j) pairs swaps each element twice, returning the matrix to its original state.

items.why: State-space matrix construction — positions form the state space, moves define the transition matrix, exponentiation counts paths returning to origin.
